{{Short description|Array of line segments normal to points of a square lattice}}
{{distinguish|Orchard-planting problem}}
[[Image:Euclid's_Orchard.svg|thumb|Plan view of one corner of Euclid's orchard, in which trees are labelled with the ''x'' co-ordinate of their projection on the plane {{math|1=''x'' + ''y'' = 1}}.]]

In [[mathematics]], informally speaking, '''Euclid's orchard''' is an array of one-dimensional "trees" of unit height planted at the lattice points in one quadrant of a [[square lattice]].<ref>{{MathWorld|urlname=EuclidsOrchard|title=Euclid's Orchard}}</ref> More formally, Euclid's orchard is the set of line segments from {{math|(''x'', ''y'', 0)}} to {{math|(''x'', ''y'', 1)}}, where {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}} are positive [[integer]]s.

[[Image:Euclid_orchard_trimetric.svg|thumb|left|One corner of Euclid's orchard {{nowrap|&ndash; as the array is}} 2-dimensional, the proportion of trees being visible from the origin (blue) tends towards {{nowrap|1={{sfrac|[[particular values of the Riemann zeta function#Even_positive_integers|&zeta;(2)]]}} = {{sfrac|6|{{pi}}<sup>2</sup>}} &asymp; 60.8% <ref>{{MathWorld|urlname=VisiblePoint|title=Visible point}}</ref>}}]]
[[Image:Euclid's Orchard (perspective).svg|thumb|Perspective view of Euclid's orchard from the origin. Red trees denote rows two off the main diagonal.]]

The trees visible from the origin are those at lattice points {{math|(''x'', ''y'', 0)}}, where {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}} are [[coprime]], i.e., where the fraction {{math|{{sfrac|''x''|''y''}}}} is in [[Irreducible fraction|reduced form]]. The name ''Euclid's orchard'' is derived from the [[Euclidean algorithm]].

If the orchard is [[3D projection|projected]] relative to the origin onto the plane {{math|1=''x'' + ''y'' = 1}} (or, equivalently, drawn in [[perspective (graphical)|perspective]] from a viewpoint at the origin) the tops of the trees form a graph of [[Thomae's function]]. The point {{math|(''x'', ''y'', 1)}} projects to

: <math>\left ( \frac {x}{x+y}, \frac {y}{x+y}, \frac {1}{x+y} \right ).</math> 

The solution to the [[Basel problem]] can be used to show that the proportion of points in the {{tmath|n\times n}} grid that have trees on them is approximately <math>\tfrac{6}{\pi^2}</math> and that the error of this approximation goes to zero in the [[Limit (mathematics)|limit]] as {{mvar|n}} goes to infinity.<ref>{{cite book|contribution=Chapter 9: Sneaky segments|pages=101–106|title=Circle in a Box|series=MSRI Mathematical Circles Library|first=Sam|last=Vandervelde|publisher=Mathematical Sciences Research Institute and American Mathematical Society|year=2009}}</ref>
